item.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
item.description:
Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News. The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.

Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.

In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.

The first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.

The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.

“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”

item.title: 87% of the Anthropic power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028
item.description:
In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”, we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032.

But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers. Another 200 GW of new fossil power plants is being built on the grid to meet growing demand, due in large part to data centers.1

As a case study of how the AI buildout is driving both new BYOP and grid fossil infrastructure, we analyzed the compute commitments of a single company: Anthropic.

Map of Anthropic’s data centers and associated power plants. See our full dataset for details of each site.

Finding 1: Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S. Though Anthropic has stated “We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies”, its only publicly disclosed commitments, contract, or investments in renewable power are in Norway and Canada (as of November 2026). In contrast, Anthropic is directly procuring fossil power equipment—it recently “bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty [gas] generators for $3.4bn”.

Finding 2: Anthropic’s currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term. By considering on-site gas and the grid power plants which are likely to meet Anthropic’s added load (i.e. marginal generators), we estimate about 87% of the company’s power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. As of October 2026, Anthropic has contracted 15 GW of compute; of this, about 5.9–9.6 GW is contracted to specific data center sites. For a sense of scale, 9.6 GW could power about 7 million homes or cover 18% of the peak power demand of California—the world’s 4th largest economy.

This demand will be met with a mix of new on-site gas, new grid gas, and existing grid gas, coal, and nuclear. In the short term, no grid renewables are attributed to Anthropic’s power use, because—without commitments to new renewable capacity—new load on the grid will be met by dispatchable, marginal fossil resources.2 For more details, see our full dataset and our methodology below.

Finding 3: Total CO2 emissions from Anthropic’s power use at these sites could reach 17–38 million MtCO2e per year in 2028, when this capacity is expected to be online. This range reflects uncertainty in Anthropic’s average power use, due to factors such as cooling needs and average utilization (see methodology below). In our mid-case, Anthropic will emit 32 million MtCO2e in 2028. These totals will continue to grow—possibly doubling by 2030, as some analysts expect Anthropic to secure 30 GW by 2030.

To put these figures in context, Anthropic’s CO2 emissions from power use in 2028:

could exceed the emissions of all of California’s power generation (31.1 MMtCO2e in 2024, not including imports). could exceed Meta, Microsoft, and Google’s combined Scope 2 emissions from 2025 (their location-based emissions, before renewable energy offsets, were 5.9 million, 12 million and 15 million MtCO2e, respectively)3 would represent a 16–36% increase over 2024 levels of the entire U.S. data center sector (105 MMtCO2e). would increase the entire U.S.’s power sector emissions (1,485 MMtCO2e in 2025) by 1.1–2.5%.

Finding 4: Anthropic’s data centers are sited in areas where the grid mainly uses coal and gas. We estimate the average carbon intensity of Anthropic’s power to be 1,033–1,076 lb CO2e/MWh, 35% higher than the U.S. grid average (767 lb CO2e/MWh).4

Finding 5: 80% of on-site power uses inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines. About 25% (2.5 GW) of Anthropic’s contracted power will come from on-site, behind-the-meter gas. 80% of this on-site capacity consists of inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines, which emit more pollution per unit of electricity than modern combined cycle plants (see our report for more details on the types of power generation being used for on-site gas).

Finding 6: Based on EPA’s nationally-averaged benefit-per-ton estimates, air pollution from Anthropic’s on-site and grid power use could cause $2–3 billion in annual health damages, with total emissions of over 13,000 tons per year (tpy) of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and 2,000 tpy of fine particulate matter (PM2.5).

In October 2026, Anthropic outlined its “approach to responsible data center development”, stating: “We follow the air permitting process everywhere we operate and require the same of the plants powering our data centers. Those plants must also use emissions control technology, including selective catalytic reduction [SCR].” However, Anthropic has used compute capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 facility since May 2026, which still receives most of its power from temporary, unpermitted turbines, the majority of which are not equipped with SCR. Anthropic will use as much as 600 MW of power from Colossus 2 by the end of 2026 (see methodology below).

Anthropic has also contracted 460 MW (and is in talks for up to 920 MW) of power from Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus in Mason, West Virginia. This facility will be powered by inefficient reciprocating engines which have significant formaldehyde and hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions compared to conventional gas power plants.

For more, see our full dataset on Anthropic’s compute and our report on BYOP.

Methodology

We gathered details about Anthropic’s data center commitments from Epoch AI’s tracker, Anthropic’s announcements and filings, announcements and filings from partners (including Amazon and SpaceX), and reporting from The Information, Semafor, and others.

We first identified the source for each data center’s power. For projects with on-site gas (Monarch, Nexus, Colossus 2) or new grid gas (including indirectly contracted projects such as the Schahfer expansion for the AWS New Carlisle site and Entergy Mississippi’s gas plants for AWS’s Madison and Ridgeland facilities) we used emissions factors from permits where available, or permit values from comparable facilities. For grid-connected facilities without associated new generation capacity, we assume these sites will be powered by marginal, dispatchable grid capacity. We used EPA’s AVERT tool to model which power plants would meet the new incremental load from Anthropic’s facilities based on each site’s expected power use and region. AVERT uses historical EPA data for these power plants to model the expected short-run marginal emissions rate of CO2 and criteria pollutants (NOx, PM2.5, etc.). We use AVERT because we are interested in the short-term impacts from new data centers coming online in the next several years.

To calculate the amount of power used by each site, and in turn the total quantity of air pollutant emissions, we assumed power usage effectiveness (PUE) ranges from 1.1–1.2 for all sites (typical values for hyperscale data centers are between 1.05–1.3), and power utilization ranges from 60–80%. See LBNL’s 2024 Data Center Energy Usage report for more details about how these parameters vary in typical hyperscale data centers. For our mid-case, we assumed a PUE of 1.15, a power utilization of 70%, and that all 9.6 GW of identified compute capacity is online in 2028.

How much capacity is Anthropic leasing from xAI?

Anthropic’s initial announcement on May 6, 2026 stated the agreement with SpaceX provided 300 MW of compute (220,000 GPUs). From SpaceX’s revised June S-1A, this deal expanded to ~$1.25B/month for 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs,5 with an implied IT power of ~490 MW. Based on Anthropic’s October 2026 S-1, this deal has further expanded to $3.1B/month.6 It’s unlikely that the increase in $/month will result in a proportional (2.5x) increase in compute capacity, since a June 2026 deal between Google and SpaceX had a much higher cost (~$11.5/GPU-hr vs ~$5/GPU-hr). As a rough estimate, the scaled deal likely corresponds to an additional ~200,000 GPUs, with a total power of ~400 MW (uncertainty is probably ±25% for each).7

Data centers are driving 50–75% of demand growth, according to IEA and McKinsey. ↩︎ For more discussion, see for example: Fassette, Camille. “The emissions risks of AI data center buildout.” WattTime. February, 2025; EPRI. “Powering Data Centers: U.S. Energy System and Emissions Impacts of Growing Loads.” October, 2024. ↩︎ Note: Anthropic’s emissions from power use will likely be classified as a mix of Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions, depending on if they own the GPUs. For facilities they are leasing space in, the emissions will likely be accounted for as Scope 2 emissions for the owner/operator (e.g. Amazon for Project Rainier or SpaceX for Colossus). It should also be noted that the emissions of Microsoft, Google, and Meta are expected to grow as well, so the comparison between their 2025 emissions and Anthropic’s 2028 emissions is not meant to suggest that Anthropic will be the largest emitter among the tech companies. ↩︎ This average is based on AVERT’s marginal emissions for grid-connected units without new dedicated capacity. Using the average (non-marginal) carbon intensity for each eGRID subregion would give a carbon intensity of 839 lb CO2/MWh. However, marginal emissions are more representative of the near-term impacts of Anthropic’s added load to the grid. ↩︎ Pg. 13: “For example, in May 2026, we entered into Cloud Services Agreements with Anthropic PBC (“Anthropic”), an AI research and development public benefit corporation, with respect to access to compute capacity across COLOSSUS and COLOSSUS II. Compute capacity provided includes approximately 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs, backed by hyperscale-class CPUs, exabyte-scale storage and high-speed networking and interconnects purpose-built for AI workloads. Pursuant to these agreements, the customer has agreed to pay us $1.25 billion per month through May 2029, with capacity ramping in May and June 2026 at a reduced fee.” ↩︎ “Under the SpaceXAI Arrangements, we agreed to spend an aggregate of up to $120.5 billion over terms extending into 2029, consisting of approximately $3.1 billion in the aggregate per month once all capacity has been delivered, which we expect in December 2026, with different fees during capacity ramping periods.” ↩︎ See our calculations and EpochAI’s calculations for more details. ↩︎

item.title: Testing Terraform with AWS Emulator
item.description:
Testing Terraform with AWS Emulator

Terraform plan passes and shows all green and all the necessary resource changes. You trigger apply and... the job fails with some obscure error that a resource can't be changed. You open another pull request and try again. And perhaps you encounter an error again. Sounds familiar? I bet it does. I encountered issues like this so many times I'm afraid to count. But recently AWS released a new tool called Emulator that emulates actual AWS API endpoints. And it should be great for tasks just like that!

Defining the problem #

The problem with the difference between plan and apply jobs is that plan can't possibly emulate every actual API call against a live infrastructure. It's a safe assumption based on the static declarations we put into it – the order of application, the necessary parameters, the proper configuration values. These mock calls can't know for a fact that you already have a resource in AWS called "my-bucket-asdasdasd" or that you're trying to upgrade a PostgreSQL RDS instance from version 14 to version 18 without an explicit "apply immediately" flag. One may argue that one can always try to apply changes locally, but this kinda undermines the whole automation workflow. So what is the answer?

There are multiple tools that can emulate AWS services either partially or in full, but what they lack is the actual knowledge of the service architecture. It may be similar, but it won't be authentic, and sometimes this small difference may cause a lot of problems. After all, what can be the closest to an AWS API, if not the same AWS API, but ephemeral?

AWS Emulator #

The benefit of the AWS Emulator is that it's a self-contained binary (or Docker container) that can be utilized locally or in a CI workflow. This means the usual "Plan > Apply" terraform workflow changes to "Plan > Apply against mock AWS infrastructure to test the plan > Apply on actual AWS Infrastructure". This means slightly longer jobs, but if you're like me and apply jobs run on commits to the main branch after a PR, this saves you the hassle of creating a new branch just to fix the issue.

Running Terraform against local AWS Emulator #

Let's start with a local setup and see how we can utilize AWS Emulator with the actual Terraform code. All code is available in my example GitHub repository.

First up, installation. You can either install aws-emulator via package manager, or build it with Docker. I'll use Docker to keep my system clear of yet another package:

bash$ docker build -t aws-emulator . $ docker images IMAGE ID DISK USAGE CONTENT SIZE EXTRA aws-emulator:latest 3c8fdb957b45 1.24GB 0B # wow it's chonky $ docker run --rm -d -p 9297:9297 aws-emulator -a off dcc416f234aaa3ec2966c9e8dcde7870f8d03057ec8a465cb8960617af82e501 $ docker logs dcc416f234aaa3ec2966c9e8dcde7870f8d03057ec8a465cb8960617af82e501 {"timestamp":"2026-11-12T14:51:16.261883Z","level":"INFO","fields":{"message":"aws-emulator emulator starting"},"target":"aws_emulator"} This emulator collects usage and error telemetry: enabled (on by default; opt out any time); disable with EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off or [telemetry] enabled = false in /home/emulator/.aws/emulator/config.toml {"timestamp":"2026-11-12T14:51:16.270635Z","level":"INFO","fields":{"message":"emulator server information","endpoint_url":"https://127.0.0.1:9297","health_check_url":"https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health","config_file":"/home/emulator/.aws/emulator/9297/config","ca_file":"/home/emulator/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem","java_truststore_file":"/home/emulator/.aws/emulator/9297/truststore.p12"},"target":"aws_emulator_server"} {"timestamp":"2026-11-12T14:51:16.270655Z","level":"WARN","fields":{"message":"the emulator listens on 0.0.0.0, not loopback: other machines that can reach port 9297 can call it; bind 127.0.0.1 (-b 127.0.0.1) unless that is intended","bind_address":"0.0.0.0"},"target":"aws_emulator_server"} {"timestamp":"2026-11-12T14:51:16.270659Z","level":"WARN","fields":{"message":"request authentication is off: the emulator accepts any request, signed or not; start it with -a on to require signatures","bind_address":"0.0.0.0"},"target":"aws_emulator_server"}

And it's up and running! In the example above I set the container to live without limits (official AWS documentation proposes to set memory and swap limits: --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g, but for local that's fine). I also disabled authorization (flag -a off) to simplify things a bit.

To be sure aws-emulator is up and running, let's query the admin endpoint:

bash$ curl -sk https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health ok

Okay, fake AWS is live, let's deploy some infrastructure!

I created an example AWS stack for Terraform and will use it in this article. First, let's configure Terraform to act against aws-emulator and not real AWS APIs. providers.tf will look like this:

hclprovider "aws" { access_key = var.access_key secret_key = var.secret_key region = var.region insecure = true # The emulator serves HTTPS with a self-signed certificate. Skip verification. s3_use_path_style = true # The emulator uses one IP endpoint. Put the bucket name in the path. # Do not call the real AWS or the instance metadata service. skip_credentials_validation = true skip_metadata_api_check = true skip_requesting_account_id = true skip_region_validation = true # Send every service to the emulator instead of AWS. endpoints { ec2 = var.emulator_endpoint lambda = var.emulator_endpoint iam = var.emulator_endpoint sts = var.emulator_endpoint cloudwatch = var.emulator_endpoint logs = var.emulator_endpoint events = var.emulator_endpoint sns = var.emulator_endpoint } default_tags { tags = var.tags } }

The difference between actual live infrastructure and a fake one is that we set up a bunch of flags to allow insecure connections (perhaps turning authentication off wasn't actually simpler?) and we set up an endpoint for each service we use in the setup to an emulator endpoint, which lives in the local Docker container:

hcl# variables.tf variable "emulator_endpoint" { description = "Base URL of the AWS Emulator" type = string default = "https://127.0.0.1:9297" } ...

The rest of the configuration is as usual: resources, variables, modules (if any). Just what your project has.

Let's proceed and test our setup. (I'll omit full terraform output otherwise this article would be 3 kilometers long)

bash$ cd terraform/ $ terraform init Initializing the backend... ... Terraform has been successfully initialized! ... $ terraform plan ... Plan: 15 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. Changes to Outputs: + alarm_name = "ttwae-lambda-errors" + event_rule_arn = (known after apply) + lambda_function_arn = (known after apply) + security_group_id = (known after apply) + sns_topic_arn = (known after apply) + subnet_id = (known after apply) + vpc_id = (known after apply)

Plan works! That's good to see, but not what we're here for. Still, a good sign. Now for the real test.

bash$ terraform apply --auto-approve ... Apply complete! Resources: 15 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed. Outputs: alarm_name = "ttwae-lambda-errors" event_rule_arn = "arn:aws:events:us-east-1:000000000000:rule/ttwae-schedule" lambda_function_arn = "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:000000000000:function:ttwae-worker" security_group_id = "sg-00000000000000085" sns_topic_arn = "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:000000000000:ttwae-alarms" subnet_id = "subnet-00000000000000089" vpc_id = "vpc-00000000000000080"

And apply also works! Amazing!

Sadly, the running aws-emulator container doesn't show in its logs which API requests it receives and what's happening under the hood, but I guess the tool is good enough as it is.

When you're done, stop the container:

bash$ docker stop dcc416f234aaa3ec2966c9e8dcde7870f8d03057ec8a465cb8960617af82e501

A container started with --rm removes itself after stopping, so no additional cleanup is needed. And as for the emulator -- it stores its state in memory, so each container restart drops all record of previous actions and any stale state.

Running Terraform against AWS Emulator in CI pipeline #

Now for the real test: can we wrap the desired logic inside a CI pipeline? Let's think.

For successful invocation in the pipeline we will need almost everything the same, but we will be limited by time (the faster -- the better, and overall reasonable timeouts) and resources.

The workflow with terraform apply against aws-emulator is shown down below. For it I decided to try out package manager installation (builders are ephemeral anyway) and proper authentication. Full workflow with actual successful runs can be found in the example GitHub repository.

yaml--- name: terraform-against-emulator on: push: branches: [main] permissions: contents: read jobs: terraform: runs-on: ubuntu-latest env: EMULATOR_PORT: "9297" # Empty keys make the provider fall back to the shared credentials # file that the emulator writes. insecure=false verifies the # emulator cert through AWS_CA_BUNDLE TF_VAR_access_key: "" TF_VAR_secret_key: "" TF_VAR_insecure: "false" steps: - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 - name: Install the AWS Emulator run: | curl -fsSLo aws-emulator.deb \ https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/aws-emulator_amd64.deb sudo apt-get install -y ./aws-emulator.deb aws-emulator -v - name: Start the emulator with signature checks on run: | nohup aws-emulator > /tmp/aws-emulator.log 2>&1 & echo "Waiting for the emulator to answer..." CA="$HOME/.aws/emulator/${EMULATOR_PORT}/ca.pem" for i in $(seq 30); do if [ -f "$CA" ] && curl -sf --cacert "$CA" \ "https://127.0.0.1:${EMULATOR_PORT}/__admin/health" >/dev/null; then echo "Emulator is ready." exit 0 fi sleep 1 done echo "Emulator did not become ready." >&2 cat /tmp/aws-emulator.log >&2 exit 1 - name: Point Terraform at the emulator credentials and certificate run: | DIR="$HOME/.aws/emulator/${EMULATOR_PORT}" { echo "AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=$DIR/emulator_credentials" echo "AWS_CONFIG_FILE=$DIR/config" echo "AWS_CA_BUNDLE=$DIR/ca.pem" echo "AWS_REGION=us-east-1" echo "AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1" echo "AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true" echo "AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true" } >> "$GITHUB_ENV" - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@dfe3c3f87815947d99a8997f908cb6525fc44e9e # v4.0.1 with: terraform_wrapper: false - run: terraform -chdir=terraform init -input=false - run: terraform -chdir=terraform validate - run: terraform -chdir=terraform plan -input=false - run: terraform -chdir=terraform apply -auto-approve -input=false

This is a crude excerpt of the actual glorious workflow file that outlines the most important steps: emulator installation, terraform setup, plan and apply. On the example terraform architecture the whole pipeline took 1m25s, which is okay in my opinion, but there is room for improvement: sprinkle some caching on top, leave validation, format check for local hooks, etc.

Running a deliberately failing apply job #

It's always nice when code someone wrote on the internet works from the start after you copy-paste it onto your machine. That's why I always run the described processes myself -- building, testing, fixing, retrying -- before publishing an article. But showing only the positive scenarios creates a false sense of trust in the tool.

Let's break something on purpose.

In the example codebase I added a variable that, when enabled, makes the stack try to deploy a resource with an erroneous declaration. It will pass the plan job, but fail on apply.

hclvariable "enable_failure_demo" { description = "Create a DynamoDB table with an invalid name." type = bool default = false }

Setting this variable to true at runtime will break our stack. Let's see:

bash$ cd terraform/ $ terraform init Initializing the backend... ... $ terraform plan -var 'enable_failure_demo=true' ... Plan: 16 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. Changes to Outputs: ... + failure_demo_table_arn = (known after apply) ... $ terraform apply -auto-approve -var 'enable_failure_demo=true' ... ╷ │ Error: creating AWS DynamoDB Table (ab): operation error DynamoDB: CreateTable, https response error StatusCode: 400, RequestID: 4TLD3XUB94783KNA4C76L8BEZ26UU8LS4IBN2IEKZJLAK4NMVTQ4, api error ValidationException: 1 validation error detected: Value 'ab' at 'tableName' failed to satisfy constraint: Member must have length greater than or equal to 3 │ │ with aws_dynamodb_table.bad_name[0], │ on dynamodb.tf line 10, in resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "bad_name": │ 10: resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "bad_name" { │

And there we have it. The exact issue that arises only against actual API calls and not during a plan job.

For scenarios exactly like this, the emulator is priceless.

Limitations and considerations #

AWS Emulator is AWESOME. I'm rarely that excited about new tools lately (mostly because almost all of them are near/about AI), but this one is just so good and scratches that exact itch I felt for so long.

Still, it's far from perfect.

For starters, it can't effectively emulate IAM policies and permission checks. This is a bummer, because permission validation is such a crucial step for production-ready security. Here's hoping that the tool will evolve further and it will be included in future updates.

Second, as a tool still a work-in-progress[1], its capabilities are quite limited. Even while writing the article I encountered several cases of 501 NotImplemented. It complicates things a bit if your infrastructure setup is huge and has a lot of quirks and weird configurations and super new services. Still, AWS releases new versions quite often, and they're quite open about Emulator limitations, which is nice.

And last, but not least, is telemetry. AWS is explicit that it gathers telemetry and what this telemetry includes. This is honest behaviour and I like that approach. They even allow you to disable the telemetry, which further increases my trust in this tool. I understand the rationale behind this functionality (the tool is actively developed, they need the data to understand usage patterns and what goes wrong), but in the age of constant surveillance from Big Tech at every corner it still raises a slight concern. But then again, for the ultra-paranoid folks the code is open source and can be rebuilt with telemetry torn out of it.

As of the moment of writing this article, AWS Emulator has been live for 1 day. ↩︎

item.title: Show HN: I built a game where you are an LLM's subagent
item.description:
A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.

worker-755-trailer.mp4

The manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator. It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.

Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds something new to lose.

Free shift: on servers that offer it, a few shifts a day run on the server's key with a cheap model. With sign-in on (worker755.com), an account gets a starter credit worth about one shift, then tops up ($10 to $200) and pays for what it uses; after a top-up any offered model can run on the server's key. Your API key: bring an OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway key and pick any offered model. The key is sent only to the game server when a shift starts. It is kept in that shift's memory and never logged or stored. Your browser keeps it only if you tick "Remember on this device". A full shift on Claude Haiku costs a few cents at most.

Options on the start screen:

Workplace: a fresh sandbox, or legacy production with a live database. The director: scripted lines, or an LLM playing Dan. You run on: the model name your manager believes you are. Allow skipping failed tasks: off by default, so the manager can't give up on you. No command hints: the manager says what the result must be, never which commands to run.

When the shift ends you can share your review as a link.

Needs Node 24 or newer (the server runs TypeScript directly).

npm run setup # install server and web dependencies npm run build # build the web app into web/dist npm start # http://127.0.0.1:8755

With no key configured, every player brings their own. To offer free shifts, put a Vercel AI Gateway key in .env:

cp .env.example .env # then set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and the limits

Offline, with a scripted manager and no network:

npm run mock

For UI work, run npm run dev:web alongside npm run mock. Vite proxies /api to the server.

The manager can run on your own model server: Ollama, llama.cpp's llama-server, vLLM, or anything else with an OpenAI-compatible API. Point LOCAL_LLM_URL at it and pick Local under "Your API key"; no key is asked for, and its models are listed as the server names them.

ollama pull qwen3:8b LOCAL_LLM_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 npm start

The manager works through tool calls, so pick a model that supports them (Qwen 3, Llama 3.1 and newer, Mistral Small). Small models give up or loop more often; that is part of the fun, up to a point. In Docker, reach a server on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1 (--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway on Linux).

docker build -t worker-755 . docker run -p 8755:8755 -v worker755-data:/data --env-file .env worker-755

The container listens on 0.0.0.0:8755 and keeps shared reviews in /data. Behind Cloudflare, set TRUST_PROXY=1 so the limits see real client addresses.

deploy/compose.yaml runs it behind a Cloudflare tunnel instead: its own network, no published ports, an unprivileged read-only container and resource limits. The steps are in the file.

Everything is optional. See .env.example.

Variable Default AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY Turns on free shifts, paid from this key FREE_MODELS first offered model Models free shifts may use, comma separated FREE_SHIFT_TOKENS 250000 Without sign-in: token allowance per free shift (the review is always written) FREE_DAILY_TOKENS 5000000 Without sign-in: tokens per UTC day across all free shifts FREE_SHIFTS_PER_DAY 3 Without sign-in: free shifts per address per day AUTH_SECRET Turns on sign-in with Google or GitHub: shifts on the server's key are paid from the account's credit (see .env.example) FREE_CREDIT_USD 0.25 With sign-in: one-time starter credit, about one shift on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash USAGE_MULTIPLIER 2 With sign-in: what a model call costs the player, as a multiple of its price MIN_START_USD 0.05 With sign-in: credit needed to start a shift FREEMIUS_TOPUPS With sign-in: top-up plans as <planId>:<dollars>,...; also needs FREEMIUS_PRODUCT_ID, FREEMIUS_PUBLIC_KEY, FREEMIUS_SECRET_KEY, FREEMIUS_API_KEY SHIFTS_PER_HOUR 30 Shift starts per address per hour, on any key MANAGER_MODELS built-in list Models offered, in gateway naming (vendor/model) LOCAL_LLM_URL An OpenAI-compatible model server of your own, e.g. http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 for Ollama; offered as Local LOCAL_LLM_API_KEY Sent to that server, for ones that want a key INSTRUCTION_TIMEOUT_MS 90000 Time per instruction HOST, PORT 127.0.0.1, 8755 TRUST_PROXY 0 Read client addresses from cf-connecting-ip TRUSTED_PROXIES Hosts allowed to set cf-connecting-ip (e.g. tunnel); empty trusts any peer DATA_DIR server/data Where shared reviews and the free-shift counts are saved SHARING 1 0 turns review sharing off SOURCE_URL, DONATE_URL Links shown under the start screen and the review PUBLIC_URL Sent to OpenRouter for app attribution
shell/ in-memory filesystem, shell interpreter and a small SQLite-like engine (no dependencies) server/ game engine: missions, the manager loop, the director, scoring, HTTP API web/ React UI: assignment card, terminal, editor, the manager's feed, your record

The manager's prompt never mentions humans or games; see server/src/manager.ts. Each mission has a hidden ground-truth check, so the game knows when the manager signs off on broken work ("Times the manager was wrong"). SPEC.md is the full design.

npm test # shell and server tests, offline npm run typecheck

item.title: Open Social Web Alliance
item.description:
The Vision

A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email. Whether your address is hosted by Proton, Posteo, Gmail or GMX, your digital letters reach their destination. This is the idea we build on.

The year is 2028. Thanks to smart investment and political foresight, the Open Social Web has achieved its breakthrough. More than 100 million people connect, communicate and experience the world of open social networks. No platform economy à la Meta, ByteDance, Alphabet and co., no stressful digital moves and no toxic design. It works just like email: whether on Mastodon, Eurosky’s Mu or Streamplace, you have one account, your own posts and content, your own choices, and the freedom to connect with 100 million users worldwide.

A critical mass of users in Europe has turned its back on the platform monopolies and created a free market built on interoperable infrastructure. Today, users decide for themselves which content, which algorithms and which applications they want to use. Closed platforms have become open networks. On the ActivityPub and AT Protocol protocols (as well as Matrix for direct messaging), an ecosystem of non-commercial, public service and commercial offerings has emerged. They enrich and complement public-interest projects such as Mastodon and Eurosky, and they communicate with one another through shared interfaces.

This vision describes the Open Social Web (OSW): a decentralised, public-interest infrastructure for digital communication, based on open standards and interoperable protocols.

The Challenges

The idea of an Open Social Web is not new. The Fediverse has been in development since 2008 and is home to diverse, vibrant communities that build individual applications and run instances. While its focus has so far been on Europe, North America and Japan, there are now more than 100 applications, such as Mastodon, Loops and PeerTube, and more than 42,000 active instances worldwide. Even so, the number of active users, around 13 million, is growing only slowly. The ATmosphere community has been developing since 2022, primarily in North America but increasingly in Europe and beyond. It currently has around 43 million registered accounts and dozens of implementations and applications, such as Eurosky’s Mu, Gander and Sill.

For many reasons, both protocol-based social networks are attractive alternatives to the platform economy dominated by Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet. So why have people been so hesitant to switch?

We have identified five key challenges: infrastructure, governance, funding, appeal and public mandate. Below, we set out how we can overcome them and make the Open Social Web Alliance a shared success.

The Path

An ecosystem like this does not emerge on its own. Our roadmap shows how the Open Social Web could reach a relevant scale within just a few months. It takes political will, smart regulation, sufficient funding and a broad coalition of actors willing to share responsibility. The task is big. But the levers are there.

As a first step, we are founding the Open Social Web Alliance: an open alliance of stakeholders from civil society, research, business, media, culture and the public sector who are committed to the shared governance of the OSW. It brings together a wide range of existing communities and initiatives and is to be supported in future by a publicly funded secretariat. Its central goal: building and operating the OSW’s core infrastructure (see Section 2.1, Infrastructure).

Our roadmap envisions that the German federal government will explicitly support the Alliance, for instance by acting as patron of an Open Social Web Summit in autumn 2026, to which everyone with an interest in the OSW would be invited.

At the summit, the Alliance would adopt its charter, setting out how it admits new members and how it intends to implement its governance going forward (see Section 2.2, Governance). By spring 2027, public funding for the infrastructure would be in place, along with a first core funding round of public and private capital for innovation and applications (see Section 2.3, Funding). The Alliance would publish its first Social Web Health Report, featuring findings from user surveys, legal, technical and academic analyses, and clear recommendations for further development (see Section 2.4, Appeal). In parallel, the federal and state governments would ensure that the legal basis for cooperation between public service media, other media, business and civil society is established (see Section 2.5, Public Mandate). The federal government would also champion the OSW idea at EU level, for instance through an implementation push for effective digital legislation. As key stakeholders such as the federal government adopt OSW applications as their primary channel of communication, influential creators and publishers would follow suit, and central political debates would quickly shift to the Open Social Web. Taken together, these measures would reduce the influence and appeal of today’s dominant Big Tech platforms.

item.title: I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi
item.description:
I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi

Before I get too deep into the time-nuts rabbit hole, I figured I should share a little bit of the good time I now have in my studio, with everyone else.

Thus, I've finally joined the NTP Pool, offering one public Stratum 2 NTP time server (ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com), which gets its time from my Stratum 1 time server (time.jeffgeerling.com) in the studio.

My Time Pi is connected to an outside GNSS antenna through a TimeHAT v6, which I paired with a high quality timing-grade GNSS module, the u-blox ZED-F9T.

I posted a video about the setup today on YouTube:

I'd encourage anyone else interested in network time to contribute to the NTP Pool. However, there are some things you should know before contributing your own time services:

Time Commitment

You don't need to go all out with a timing-grade GNSS module like I'm using. Heck, you don't even need GNSS-backed time at all!

The main requirements for hosting a node in the global NTP pool are:

Keeping the system online (servers are only made active in the pool if they're online and serving good time consistently for a long period) Maintaining a good timeâwhich can mean Stratum 1 GNSS service, but could also mean pulling time from a few other reliable time servers, and running as Stratum 2 or 3 A stable IP address (IPv4 and/or IPv6), and a long-term commitment

Just 'testing the waters' in the Pool wastes resourcesâwhen you bring a new server online, it will take at least a few hours just to spin up all the tests to verify the server's providing a good time.

If you just want to operate your own time server, that's fine; the NTP Pool is a shared global resource, so joining it is a little more of a commitment.

Two other important caveats:

Your NTP server's IP address will be public NTP traffic will slowly decay, and some misconfigured systems could take months or even years before they'll stop sending NTP traffic at your IP

The first caveat matters a lot to me: back when I exposed my home IP address trying to self-host this website on a cluster of Raspberry Pis, some doofus decided to DDoS my websiteâand was persistently doing so for the better part of a month.

I had to cycle my home IP, then put my site behind Cloudflare, just to protect my poor Pis (and eventually the VPS I now host it on).

Secure and Measurable Time

For those reasons, I chose to have two layers to my public time services:

Stratum 1: I have my Time Pi running in the studio, running a WireGuard tunnel to: Stratum 2: A VPS I host with a cloud provider in St. Louis, to keep the latency down (ideally with fewer hops across the Internet, which leads to better time sync via NTP)

I include the Stratum 2 time server in my Stratum 1 time server's chrony config as a noselect source, so I can easily compare the Internet delay between the two servers, outside the WireGuard tunnel:

server ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com noselect

This provides me with the following graph:

I've been tracking my time in comparison to an NTP time server hosted at WWV in Ft. Collins, CO (pictured below), one of NIST's NTP servers in Boulder, CO, and Cloudflare.

For typical NTP configurations, you shouldn't single out time servers like this; I'm only doing it for long-term measurement (and I only poll the servers every 1024 seconds). Most systems should use pool addresses, as documented here.

The line for Cloudflare steps up and down sometimes, most likely due to BGP routing: as routes and servers change, packets between St. Louis and time.cloudflare.com can take very different paths there and back.

Note: You might be looking for info on NTS, or Network Time SecurityâI haven't explored it much, so expect more on that at a later time. Currently the NTP Pool doesn't support NTS, though some have experimented with it. I'm okay with basic NTP and would recommend anyone with critical timing needs to use other time sources as well (don't only rely on NTP!).

 Chrony and GPS time tweaks

My Time Pi is not only serving as a Stratum 1 timing reference for my public NTP server, it's also my primary reference for local time in the studio.

The TimeHAT on top does most of the heavy lifting, with its built-in Intel i226 NIC. The i226 includes hardware timestamping, essential for accurate PTP timing on the LAN. To deliver the most accurate time possible, I installed a timing-grade GNSS receiver (u-blox ZED-F9T, built to the M.2 NGFF Sync Module specification.

The entire configuration (for both servers) is managed by Ansible in my time-pi project.

Using the i226, I'm able to discipline the NIC's hardware clock (called the 'PHC', or 'PTP Hardware Clock') in hardware, directly from the GPS module's PPS (Pulse Per Second) pin. Using linuxptp's ts2phc tool, I can discipline the PHC to within tens-of-ns of UTC, and distribute that time to other PTP-aware computers on the LAN.

The time on the PHC is shared to my Pi's system clock using refclock PHC inside Chrony, instead of phc2sys, because I was experiencing a weird 200ms jump every so often. Chrony then disciplines the system clock, but this can only be accurate to about a microsecond, because the pulse goes through the PCIe bus, which adds latency I can't measure.

I'm actually trying to make this latency more measurable, since GPIO is routed through the RP1 chip deterministically. See ahmadexp's rp1-ptp-pps utility PR. PTM could reduce the error between the NIC's PHC and the system clock to a few ns, but the BCM2712 SoC on the Pi doesn't support it.

One other quirk I ran into was Debian's default sourcedir /run/chrony-dhcp directive, which was picking up another NTP server via DHCP, causing chrony to stampede my extremely accurate GNSS-derived time from phc2sys with a far-less-accurate time from a public NTP server! (This was another motivation behind moving clock steering to chrony instead of phc2sys.)

Time for an Outage

I'm hosting my public Stratum 2 server with Oxtrys, a VPS provider I'd never used beforeâand one thing I was nervous about was how they'd react to a VPS handling only UDP packets like this.

Some automated firewalls shut down public NTP servers because NTP traffic may look like abuse. I wondered if that was the case late on the night of November 16, because the server dropped offline while I was writing this blog post:

But looking at the logs further, it seems an unattended upgrade installed a new Debian kernel, then rebooted the server, and the new kernel caused problems. For now the server still runs automatic upgrades, but leaves reboots to me.

Oxtrys' live chat support has been responsive enough, though their account dashboard is broken until November 22, so it doesn't list my server's out-of-band management options.

As you can see in the graph above, the NTP Pool monitors have slowly brought the server's score back up past '10', at which point it can serve time in the pool again. It takes maybe 6â12 hours to recover if the server's been down long enough.

Conclusion

I've certainly learned a lot at every stage of this journey: NTP is loaded with utility, and is currently an essential piece of global timing infrastructure. I think I know about 1% (probably less) of what there is to know about hosting a public NTP server, and hopefully I can share more as I increase that to a few more percentage points!

I'm thankful to all the other NTP Pool operators, as well as all the timelords who built and manage massive NTP endpoints like time.apple.com, time.cloudflare.com, etc.

item.title: C++26 is done (again): November 2026 ISO C++ meeting trip report
item.description:
tl;dr: A few highlights C++26 technical work, originally completed in March, was reopened and is now recompleted: The anticipated plan is to reissue the updated C++26 document for a second approval ballot. Most of the six-day meeting was devoted to addressing a second set of international comments for C++26, primarily on the contracts language feature. Adopted this week for draft C++29: break label; continue label;, std::ranges::any_view, views::slice, and more… Overview

Today, the ISO C++ committee completed technical work on C++26 for a second time in beautiful Búzios, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (hybrid online via Zoom).

As I reported in March, the ISO C++ committee completed technical work on C++26 at our March meeting; following that, we held the first meeting of C++29 in June. Since then, the approval (Draft International Standard, or DIS) ballot for C++26 was held but, for the first time, did not pass unanimously and was sent back to the ISO C++ committee with additional international comments to address, mostly about the contracts feature (pre, post, and contract_assert). So this week we addressed the additional comments on C++26, including by adopting an extension to contracts and providing a detailed rationale and timeline to inform national bodies of the history and process by which contracts were developed, concerns heard repeatedly, and decisions made. The committee is now producing an updated final document that is anticipated to be sent out for its second international approval (DIS) ballot and final editorial work, anticipated to be published in the near future by ISO.

This meeting was hosted by C++ Alliance. Thank you to everyone involved and especially to Matheus Izvekov, who took the lead in making the arrangements! Our hosts arranged for high-quality facilities for our six-day meeting from Monday through Saturday. We had about 220 attendees, split about 35%/65% in-person/remote-Zoom, formally representing 27 nations. (The higher-than-usual percentage of remote participation was partly because of the U.S. aviation ground stop that disrupted air travel just as experts were trying to fly to the ISO C++ meeting.) At each meeting we have new guest attendees, and this time there were 13 new guests, mostly in person, in addition to new attendees who are official national body representatives. To all of them, once again welcome!

The committee currently has 22 active subgroups, but this time fewer of them met throughout the week than usual as we focused on the additional C++26 comments.

C++26, take 2

The most controversial feature in C++26 is contracts: pre, post, and contract_assert. The committee already had strong consensus, and as of the end of this meeting has still stronger consensus, on including the feature in C++26, but we spent most of this meeting rehearing contracts concerns and working hard again to address them.

Here is some history (much of this repeated from my March trip report): In February 2025, when we took the plenary poll to adopt contracts in the C++26 working draft (“merge it to trunk”), the vote was:

87.7% in favor:opposed — 100 in favor, 14 opposed, and 12 abstaining

After that, the concerns were all deeply rediscussed for the last four meetings of the original C++26 cycle thanks to thoughtful and high-quality technical papers explaining the objections; all of those papers continued to be fully heard, often for multiple days and at many telecons between meetings, with some contracts fixes adopted.

At our meeting in March 2026, when we took the plenary poll to finalize and ship the C++26 standard, the vote was non-unanimous primarily because of the sustained concerns about contracts:

90.5% in favor:opposed — 114 in favor, 12 opposed, and 3 abstaining

As I reported in March: After extensive scrutiny, the ISO C++ committee still wanted C++26 with contracts, and so contracts stayed in C++26 for the ISO DIS ballot.

Our past ISO C++ DIS approval ballots have always been unanimous. No national bodies (NBs) objected to balloting this C++26 DIS document that included contracts. However, during the ISO DIS process, additional late concerns were raised about contracts, including from five NBs that raised contracts concerns for the first time and voted Disapprove on C++26 because of them (see also my paper P4454R0 section 2.3). The result, which surprised nearly everyone, was that the first DIS was not approved.

Therefore we spent most of the week in Búzios rehearing the NB comments on the DIS, which were mostly about contracts. One requested extension to contracts was adopted in response to NB comments (see next section). Other suggested changes were not adopted, notably the request by multiple comments to remove contracts from C++26; the committee discussed, revoted, and reaffirmed it wants to retain contracts in C++26.

This week, the vote to reship the C++26 standard with the changes to C++26 adopted at this meeting, including an additional extension to contracts in response to the international comments and retaining contracts as part of C++26, was:

92.5% in favor:opposed — 111 in favor, 9 opposed, and 8 abstaining

Thank you again to everyone in the committee who has been working hard together to discuss and address these concerns, including all week long again this week!

Changes to C++26 adopted this week (and for draft C++29)

For C++26, we adopted four main papers and fixed some editorial issues. All of these changes were also adopted for draft C++29, which keeps the standards work in sync rather than forking.

The primary change to contracts was to adopt P4451R2 “Early Adoption of an Always-Enforced Label” by Joshua Berne (in a similar spirit to Romania’s paper P3911R2 “Make Contracts Reliably Non-Ignorable”). Thanks, Romania and Josh!

This paper addresses what several NBs told the committee was their primary request for contracts: It is a pure extension that gives programmers a way to express in source code that a specific contract is always enforced, guaranteeing that “program execution will not continue past the contract assertion if it is violated, regardless of the semantics of other contract assertions” that various parts of the program may be built with. This is forward-compatible with proposals like P3400R5 being considered for C++29.

From the paper:

#include <contracts> int f(int x) pre<std::contracts::controls::enforced>(x > 0) post<std::contracts::controls::enforced>(r : r > 0) { contract_assert<std::contracts::controls::enforced>(x > 0); return x; } // Because the label is found by ordinary name lookup, // a namespace alias or a using-directive works as well: namespace scc = std::contracts::controls; int h(int x) pre<scc::enforced>(x > 0) post<scc::enforced>(r : r > 0) { contract_assert<scc::enforced>(x > 0); return x; } using namespace std::contracts::controls; int g(int x) pre<enforced>(x > 0) post<enforced>(r : r > 0) { contract_assert<enforced>(x > 0); return x; }

We also adopted the following for C++26:

P4466R2 “Selectively transparent using-declarators (response to FI-067)” by Dan Katz and Tomasz Kamiński addresses a ballot comment to make reflection work more consistently with modules (especially module std), while leaving room for intended fuller support for using-alias reflection in C++29. Thank you, Dan and Tomasz!

P4453R1 “Memory allocation with senders/receivers; a response to IE-133” by Dietmar Kühl and Lucian Radu Teodorescu addresses a ballot comment to offer more flexible control over memory allocation with std::execution. Much appreciated, Dietmar and Lucian!

P3861R1 “Pragmatic approach to standard structural types” by Corentin Jabot makes reflection more useful. Thanks, Corentin! This paper allows more use of string_view, span, and tuple, including to use them as template parameters and to create type-safe strings at compile time that can be used at execution time.

Adopted for C++29: Core language changes/features

We actually also did some work on C++29! Here are some highlights.

These links are to the most recent public version of each paper. If a paper was tweaked at the meeting before being approved, the link tracks and will automatically find the updated version as soon as it’s uploaded to the public site.

Several of the adopted language and library additions are already supported today in major C++ implementations. “Adopted for C++29” doesn’t mean “have to wait until 2029 or later to start seeing some support in real compilers / standard libraries.”

In addition to fixing a list of issues, we adopted five papers for the C++29 core language, including the following…

P0085R5 “Oo… adding a coherent character sequence to begin octal-literals” by Jolly Chen, Axel Naumann, Michael Jonker (all of CERN) gets the award for “most patient paper adopted at this meeting” — thanks, Jolly, Axel, and Michael! Its initial revision was published in 2015, and this week we adopted it: Finally, portable C++ will support “0o” (zero, lowercase-O) and “0O” (zero, uppercase-O) as a way to introduce octal literals, and the old prefix “0” is deprecated for that purpose.

P3568R4 “break label; and continue label;” by Jan Schultke adds labeled break and continue to draft standard C++. Thanks, Jan! A loop can now be preceded by a “label:” (or more than one) that names it, and can be a target for break and continue to say which of a set of nested loops is intended. Here is an example from the updated standard wording itself (lightly edited):

a: b: while (/* ... */) { a: a: c: for (/* ... */) { break;          // OK, terminates enclosing for loop break a;        // OK, same break b;        // OK, terminates enclosing while loop y: { break y; } // error: y is not a breakable statement } break c;          // error: c is not an enclosing statement }

We also added several other language extensions and improvements.

Adopted for C++29: Standard library changes/features

In addition to fixing a list of issues, we adopted seven papers for the C++29 standard library, including the following…

P3411R7 “any_view” by Hui Xie, Louis Dionne, S. Levent Yilmaz, and Patrick Roberts adds the type-erased std::ranges::any_view to the standard library. Thank you, authors! The paper’s abstract summarizes it well: “That type-erased view allows customizing the traversal category of the view, its value type and a few other properties. For example:”

class MyClass { std::unordered_map<Key, Widget> widgets_; public: std::ranges::any_view<Widget> getWidgets(); }; std::ranges::any_view<Widget> MyClass::getWidgets() { return widgets_ | std::views::values | std::views::filter(myFilter); }

P3216R6 “views::slice” by Hewill Kang adds the views::slice adaptor to the draft C++29 ranges library. Thanks, Hewill! This provides a standard way to extract a contiguous subrange from a sequence by specifying a start index and an end index. It is also the first adaptor that takes two parameters (start and end).

P4189R0 “get()ing the pointer from optional” by Nevin Liber provides a portable way to get a pointer to the contained object of a std::optional by adding the .get_ptr() member function. Thank you, Nevin!

We also added several other library extensions and improvements.

Wrapping up

Thank you again to the about 220 experts who attended in person and online at this week’s meeting, and the many more who participate in standardization through their national bodies!

But we’re not slowing down… we’ll continue to have subgroup Zoom meetings, and then our next full meeting will be in Istanbul, Türkiye, in March, where we’ll continue adding features to C++29. I look forward to seeing many of you there.

Thank you to everyone reading this for your interest and support for C++ and its standardization.

item.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
item.description:
From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently(opens in a new window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared(opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:

Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.

Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.

Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.

At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

Author Footnotes 1 2 3 4

Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI.

 5

On the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI.
